text: Every baby dinosaur hatched from an egg. Some, like many of the giant long-necks, seem to have been left to look after themselves from the start. Others, especially the bird-like dinosaurs, had parents that [[@wild-penguin-dads|sat on their nests]], the way birds do now.

Once hatched, dinosaur babies grew fast. [[@bones-growth|Rings inside their bones]] show that a young T. rex went through a huge [[@body-growth-spurts|growth spurt]] in its teenage years. Most dinosaurs reached adult size in their teens or twenties, far quicker than big [[reptile|reptiles]] today.

st.prompt: How do scientists work out how old a dinosaur was when it died?

options.t: By counting growth rings inside its bones
By counting the teeth in its mouth
By measuring how long its tail was

st.reveal: Many bones lay down a ring each year, like a tree trunk. Scientists cut a thin slice of bone, look at it under a microscope and count the rings. The spacing also shows when the animal grew fast and when it slowed down.

myth: Oviraptor was an egg thief that raided other dinosaurs' nests.

It was named "egg thief" in 1924 because it was found on top of eggs. In the 1990s, fossils showed its relatives sitting on nests of their own eggs, arms spread like a hen. It was a parent, not a thief.

sec.t:
In 1978, the owner of a small rock shop in Montana showed some tiny bones to the [[fossil|fossil]] hunter Jack Horner and his friend Bob Makela. They had come from a nest with the bones of many babies inside. Nearby, the pair later found a hill so full of eggs and nests that it became known as Egg Mountain.

The babies were too big to be newly hatched, so they seem to have stayed in the nest for a while. Horner suggested their parents brought them food. He named the dinosaur Maiasaura, "good mother lizard". Not every scientist agrees the babies were fed, but Maiasaura is now the state fossil of [[@states-usa|Montana]].

Dinosaur eggs were slow. [[@teeth|Baby teeth]] inside fossil eggs have tiny daily growth lines, like ticks on a calendar. Counting them showed that some dinosaur embryos spent around three to six months in the egg. A [[@eggs|hen's egg]] hatches in about three weeks.

Long-necked [[sauropod|sauropods]] laid many eggs in pits and covered them with soil and plants. In India, the [[@dino-eggs|titanosaur nests]] of the Narmada valley held several eggs each, and some held more than a dozen. A long wait in an unguarded nest was risky, so laying lots of eggs helped. It is a plan [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] still use.

Scientists cut thin slices from fossil bones and count the yearly growth rings. In 2004, a study of tyrannosaur bones found that a T. rex grew slowly for its first ten years or so. Then, as a teenager, it gained about 2 kg a day for several years. By about 20 it was fully grown, around the weight of an elephant.

A baby titanosaur from Madagascar, about the size of a big dog, had legs already built for walking long distances. It was probably on its own soon after hatching. Small and alone, baby dinosaurs were easy prey, and many never grew up at all.

Dinosaur families were probably as varied as animal families today. [[@croc-ancient|Crocodiles]], the dinosaurs' living cousins, guard their nests and carry their hatchlings gently in their jaws. Most birds feed their chicks for weeks. One fossil from China shows more than 30 young Psittacosaurus huddled together with one older animal. Some scientists see a babysitter. Others think the group simply died together.

text: You can see dinosaurs in natural history museums across the world. Some of the most famous are in the United States, which has a huge number of dinosaur [[fossil|fossils]]. The American Museum of Natural History in [[@new-york|New York]], the Field Museum in [[@chicago|Chicago]] and the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]]'s National Museum of Natural History in Washington, DC all have giant halls of skeletons.

India has dinosaur fossils too. In [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], the Indian Statistical Institute displays a skeleton of Barapasaurus, a long-necked plant-eater found in Telangana. In Gujarat and [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], fossil parks let you see [[@dino-eggs|dinosaur eggs]] and bones where they were found.

st.reveal: Real fossils are rock, heavy and sometimes fragile. Museums often display casts made from moulds of the real bones, while the originals are kept safely where scientists can study them. Good museums label which parts are real.

myth: The dinosaur skeletons in museums are always made of the real bones.

Many are casts, or a mix of real bones and casts to fill missing parts. Museums do this to protect the originals, to make skeletons light enough to mount, and so that several museums can display the same famous dinosaur.

sec.t:
Dinosaur fossils are rarely found as complete skeletons. Usually scientists find scattered bones, often broken, and spend years cleaning them out of rock. Then they work out how the bones fit, using other skeletons and living animals such as birds and crocodiles as guides.

Because real fossil bones are made of rock, they can be very heavy. So museums often show casts. A mould is taken from each real bone, then filled with lightweight resin or plaster. Missing bones are sculpted from similar animals. Steel frames, often hidden inside, hold the skeleton up.

The first dinosaur skeleton mounted for the public was Hadrosaurus, a duck-billed dinosaur shown at the Academy of Natural Sciences in [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|Philadelphia]] in 1868. Crowds flocked to see it.

{{story:museums}}

Sue, at Chicago's Field Museum, is one of the largest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. It was dug up in South Dakota in 1990 and named after the [[@dino-hunters|fossil hunter]] Sue Hendrickson. In 1997, the museum bought it at auction for over 8 million US dollars. Nobody knows if Sue was male or female.

The American Museum of Natural History displays a cast of Patagotitan, a giant plant-eater from Argentina. It is about 37 m long, so long that its head pokes out of the room it stands in. In Washington, DC, the Smithsonian reopened its dinosaur hall in 2019 with a real T. rex skeleton on loan from the US government, posed eating a [[@triceratops-horns|Triceratops]].

India's dinosaur story is less famous but rich. The skeleton of [[@barapasaurus|Barapasaurus]] at the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata was assembled from bones dug up from the late 1950s onwards in the Pranhita-Godavari valley, in what is now Telangana.

At Raiyoli near Balasinor in Gujarat, a fossil park protects the place where hundreds of dinosaur eggs and the bones of [[@rajasaurus|Rajasaurus]], a meat-eater with a small horn, were found. In Dhar district in Madhya Pradesh, another fossil park shows nests of titanosaur eggs. Seeing fossils where they lay gives a sense of how long ago, and how near, those animals were.

Modern museums do more than display skeletons. Many have glass-walled labs where you can watch scientists clean fossils with tiny drills and brushes. Others use screens to show how dinosaurs moved and what colours they may have been. Some let visitors touch a real fossil, smoothed by thousands of hands, so you can feel bone that turned to stone millions of years ago.

In London, the Natural History Museum's famous Diplodocus cast, "Dippy", toured Britain after 2017, while a real [[@blue-whale|blue whale]] skeleton took its place in the main hall. Whether in London, Chicago or Kolkata, a museum is the closest any of us will get to standing beside a living dinosaur.

text: Most dead animals rot or get eaten. A [[fossil|fossil]] forms only when something gets buried fast, in mud, sand or volcanic ash.
Water seeping through the [[sediment|sediment]] carries [[mineral|minerals]]. They fill the tiny holes in the bone and harden into stone.

Much later, [[erosion|erosion]] uncovers it, and someone has to be lucky enough to spot it. The whole process usually takes millions of years, though some fossils form much faster in the right conditions.

Most fossils are rock. Minerals have filled or replaced the original bone, keeping its shape. Many skeletons on display are also casts, copies made from moulds of the real fossils.

sec.h: Why most things never become fossils
sec.t:
When an animal dies, scavengers, [[bacteria|bacteria]], sun and rain usually destroy it within weeks. Hard parts like bones, teeth and shells last longest, so they're what we usually find. Soft animals, like worms and jellyfish, almost never fossilise.

Where an animal lived matters too. Seas, lakes and river [[@floods-why|floods]] lay down mud again and again, burying things quickly. Mountains and forests do the opposite: they wear away. That is why sea creatures are the most common fossils, and why we know so little about animals that lived on hills.

If a body is quickly covered by [[sediment|sediment]], it's protected. Over time, groundwater carries [[dissolve|dissolved]] [[mineral|minerals]] into the tiny spaces in bone and leaves them behind, like filling a sponge with stone. This is called permineralisation.

Sometimes the original material dissolves completely and is replaced, grain by grain, by a different mineral. In other cases the body dissolves away and leaves a hollow in the rock, called a mould. If the hollow later fills with minerals, it makes a natural cast. Layers of mud pressed down become rock themselves, as explained in [[@rocks-types|types of rock]].

Trees can fossilise too. At Petrified Forest National Park in [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]], whole logs over 200 million years old have turned to colourful quartz. India has its own [[@earth-stone-forests|stone forests]]. The Akal Wood Fossil Park near Jaisalmer has fossil tree trunks from the Jurassic, when the area was near a coast. The Mandla Plant Fossils National Park in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] holds fossil plants from around the end of the age of dinosaurs.

{{story:ancient-env}}

Footprints pressed into mud, burrows, eggs and even poo can become fossils. These are called trace fossils, because they show what animals did rather than what they looked like. Insects trapped in tree resin become [[@amber-fossils|amber fossils]].

Some fossils hardly change at all. [[@mammoths|Woolly mammoths]] have been found frozen in the ground in Siberia, with skin and hair. At [[@la-brea|La Brea]] in Los Angeles, animals sank into sticky tar that soaked into their bones and preserved them. Very fine mud or ash can even keep traces of feathers and [[@dino-colors|colour]].

Fossils are found where old rock layers are exposed: cliffs, riverbanks, quarries and deserts. Deserts are especially good, because there are few plants to hide the rock. To know their age, scientists read the rock layers around them.

Finding a fossil is only the start. Diggers wrap fragile bones in plaster jackets, like a cast on a broken arm, before carrying them to a lab. There, people clean away the rock with tiny drills and brushes, sometimes for months. A big skeleton can take years to prepare. Then scientists can finally study it, and [[@dino-museums|museums]] may make lightweight casts to put on display while the real bones are kept safe in storage.

text: A rainbow forms when sunlight shines into raindrops. Each drop works like a tiny [[prism|prism]]. As light enters the drop, it bends. It bounces off the back of the drop and bends again on the way out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so white sunlight spreads out into a band of colours.
You only see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and rain is falling in front. The light comes back towards you at an angle of about 42°, which is why rainbows always form a curved arc.

sec.t:
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of all the colours of the rainbow. In the 1660s, Isaac Newton shone sunlight through a glass prism in a darkened room in England. The light spread into a band of colours on the wall. When he passed those colours through a second prism, they joined back into white light.

That showed the colours were already inside white light, and the prism was only separating them. Newton wrote about it in his book *Opticks*. You can read more about [[@colour-mix|mixing light]] and why it behaves differently from paint.

When light passes from air into water, it slows down and changes direction. This bending is called [[refraction|refraction]]. It is the same effect that makes a straw look bent in a glass of water, and that [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] use to focus light.

Violet light bends a little more than red light. So when sunlight enters a raindrop, the colours begin to separate. The light reflects off the inside back of the drop, then bends again as it leaves. Red light comes out at about 42° from the direction of the incoming sunlight, violet at about 40°, and the other colours in between.

Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears outside the first. Its light has bounced twice inside each raindrop, which flips the order of the colours: red is on the inside, violet on the outside. It sits at about 51°.

Look between the two bows and the sky is darker than elsewhere. This band is called Alexander's dark band, after the Greek thinker Alexander of Aphrodisias, who described it about 1,800 years ago.

Rainbows need low sunshine. If the Sun is higher than about 42° in the sky, the rainbow would be below the horizon. So in India, the best time is often a [[monsoon|monsoon]] afternoon when the clouds break and the Sun shines in late in the day. In the USA, [[@thunderstorms|summer thunderstorms]] in the late afternoon often leave rainbows behind.

[[@waterfalls|Waterfalls]] make rainbows too. On sunny days, the spray at [[@niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]] or at Jog Falls in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] often holds a rainbow. And on clear moonlit nights with rain, a pale moonbow can appear. It looks almost white to our eyes, because our eyes don't see colour well in dim light.

In India, many children learn VIBGYOR: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. In the USA, they learn ROY G. BIV, the same colours in reverse. Both come from Newton's list. Other cultures have counted the colours differently, and some languages name five or six. The colours themselves don't change, only the words we use for them.

text: Sand is rock that has been broken into tiny pieces. [[geologist|Geologists]] call any grain between about 0.06 mm and 2 mm wide "sand", whatever it is made of.

Most sand starts in mountains. Rain, ice, frost and plants slowly crack rocks like [[granite|granite]] apart, a process called [[weathering|weathering]]. Rivers carry the loose bits downstream, bumping and grinding them smaller along the way. Softer minerals wear away, but quartz is hard and doesn't [[dissolve|dissolve]] easily, so it survives. That is why most beach and river sand is mainly quartz.
Some sand has a very different story. It can come from [[@volcano|volcanoes]], from broken shells and coral, or even from the guts of fish.

st.prompt: Deserts are full of sand. Why do builders in desert countries often buy sand from elsewhere for concrete?

st.reveal: Wind tumbles desert grains for thousands of years until they are round and polished, like tiny marbles. In concrete, rougher, more angular grains from rivers and the sea grip each other better.

d.try: Collect a spoonful of sand from a few different places, like a beach, a riverbank, a sandpit or a building site, with an adult. Spread each on dark paper and look at it under a magnifying glass. Compare colours, shapes and sizes, and look for bits of shell.
myth: All sand is basically the same stuff.

Sand is defined by grain size, not by what it is made of. It can be quartz, volcanic rock, coral, shells, gypsum or even tiny green crystals, which is why beaches come in white, black, pink, gold and green.
facts: making concrete for buildings and roads

sec.t:
A grain of sand on a beach in [[@odisha|Odisha]] might have started as part of a rock high in the Himalayas. Rivers such as the Ganga and Brahmaputra carry enormous loads of sand and silt from the mountains, which is why they look brown during the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. Those [[@rivers-himalaya|Himalayan rivers]] drop much of it where they slow down and meet the sea, building huge deltas.

Waves and currents then spread the sand along the coast. The trip can take thousands or even millions of years, as grains are buried, lifted and washed onwards again.

On young volcanic islands, there hasn't been time for quartz sand to arrive. Instead, waves smash cooled [[lava|lava]] into black crumbs. [[@beaches|Beaches]] on the Big Island of [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]] and in Iceland are jet black for this reason.

On coral islands like the [[@maldives|Maldives]], the sand is mostly broken bits of coral and shells. Parrotfish help. They scrape at coral and [[algae|algae]] with beak-like teeth, grind up the hard parts, and pass them out as fine white sand. By some estimates, a single large parrotfish can make hundreds of kilograms of sand a year.

Some beaches in Bermuda look pink, thanks to the shells of tiny red sea creatures. Papakōlea Beach in Hawaii is green, from crystals of a volcanic mineral called olivine. At White Sands in New Mexico, the [[@earth-weird-moving-dunes|dunes]] are made of gypsum, not quartz.

{{story:coral-reefs}}

After water, sand and gravel are among the most used natural materials on Earth. Mixed with cement, gravel and water, it becomes concrete. Every flyover, [[@metro-trains|metro line]] and tall building in cities from Bengaluru to Chicago depends on it, including [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]]. Melted down, quartz sand [[@glass-made|becomes glass]], and purified, it gives the silicon used to make [[@chips-silicon|computer chips]].

A 2019 report by the United Nations Environment Programme warned that people are taking sand from rivers and beaches faster than nature replaces it. In India, as in many countries, illegal sand mining from riverbeds is a serious problem. It can deepen rivers, weaken bridges and wash away farmland.

You might think deserts could solve the shortage. But wind-blown desert grains are worn smooth and round, like tiny marbles. They roll past each other instead of locking together, so they make weak concrete. Builders prefer the rough, angular grains found in rivers and on some coasts.

So even countries surrounded by sand dunes sometimes buy sand from far away. Sand that formed over millions of years is now shipped around the world like any other cargo.

sec.h: तारा ब्लैक होल कैसे बनता है
sec.t:
तारा अपनी पूरी ज़िंदगी एक रस्साकशी में बिताता है। गुरुत्वाकर्षण उसकी गैस को अंदर खींचता है, और उसके केंद्र की गर्मी बाहर धकेलती है। ईंधन ख़त्म होते ही धक्का कमज़ोर पड़ जाता है और गुरुत्वाकर्षण जीत जाता है।

सूरज जैसा तारा आख़िर में एक [[@star-life-cycle|सफ़ेद बौना]] बन जाता है, मोटे तौर पर धरती जितना। इससे कहीं भारी तारा [[@supernova|सुपरनोवा]] बनकर फट पड़ता है। अगर पीछे बचा केंद्र काफ़ी भारी हो, तो उसे सिकुड़ने से कोई नहीं रोक सकता। सूरज को ब्लैक होल बनाने के लिए तुम्हें उसे दबाकर बस लगभग 6 किलोमीटर चौड़ी गेंद बनाना पड़ेगा, कई कस्बों से भी छोटी। पूरी कहानी [[@stars-born|तारे कैसे जीते और मरते हैं]] में पढ़ो।

ब्लैक होल को खुद नहीं देखा जा सकता। पर उसके चारों ओर घूमती गैस आपस में टकराकर बेहद गर्म हो जाती है, और चमकने लगती है।

2017 में वैज्ञानिकों ने हवाई, स्पेन, चिली और मेक्सिको जैसी एक-दूसरे से बहुत दूर की जगहों पर लगी रेडियो [[@telescopes-how|दूरबीनों]] को आपस में जोड़ा। मिलकर काम करते हुए वे धरती जितनी बड़ी एक अकेली डिश की तरह बन गईं। 2019 में उन्होंने नतीजा जारी किया: लगभग 5.5 करोड़ [[lightyear|प्रकाश-वर्ष]] दूर M87 आकाशगंगा के केंद्र में बैठे ब्लैक होल के चारों ओर एक चमकते नारंगी छल्ले की तस्वीर। उस ब्लैक होल का वज़न लगभग 6.5 अरब सूरजों जितना है।

हमारी अपनी [[@milky-way|आकाशगंगा]] के केंद्र में सैजिटेरियस A* नाम का एक ब्लैक होल बैठा है, जिसका द्रव्यमान सूरज का लगभग 40 लाख गुना है। दशकों तक खगोलशास्त्री वहाँ एक अदृश्य बिंदु के चारों ओर दौड़ते तारों पर नज़र रखते रहे। अमेरिका की आंद्रेया गेज़ और जर्मनी के राइनहार्ड गेन्ज़ेल को यह दिखाने के लिए 2020 का नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला कि बीच में कोई विशाल चीज़ छिपी है। इसकी पहली तस्वीर 2022 में आई।

यह लगभग 26,000 प्रकाश-वर्ष दूर है, हमें नुकसान पहुँचाने के लिए बहुत-बहुत दूर।

किसी छोटे ब्लैक होल के पास गुरुत्वाकर्षण तुम्हारे सिर से कहीं ज़्यादा ज़ोर से तुम्हारे पैरों को खींचेगा। अंदर गिरती कोई भी चीज़ खिंचकर लंबी और पतली हो जाती है। वैज्ञानिक इसे सचमुच "स्पेगेटीफ़िकेशन" कहते हैं, यानी सेवइयों की तरह खिंच जाना।

समय भी अजीब बर्ताव करता है। अल्बर्ट [[@einstein|आइंस्टाइन]] ने पहले ही बता दिया था कि ब्लैक होल के पास की घड़ियाँ दूर की घड़ियों से धीमी चलती हैं। 2015 में अमेरिका में LIGO नाम के दो यंत्रों ने अंतरिक्ष में उठी नन्ही लहरें महसूस कीं। ये लहरें एक अरब से भी ज़्यादा प्रकाश-वर्ष दूर दो ब्लैक होलों की टक्कर से आई थीं। भारत ने इस खोज में शामिल होने के लिए अपने यंत्र, LIGO-इंडिया, को मंज़ूरी दे दी है।

text: Astronauts eat food quite a lot like ours, packed in ways that work without [[gravity|gravity]]. On the International Space Station there are more than 100 different dishes to choose from, including scrambled eggs, curries, [[@maggi-noodles|noodles]], soups, chicken, fruit and puddings.

Most of it is either freeze-dried, which means the water has been removed so it is light and keeps for years, or heat-treated and sealed in pouches, like a ready meal. Astronauts add hot or cold water to the dried food, warm the pouches in a small oven, and eat straight from the packet with a spoon. Every few months a cargo ship brings fresh fruit and vegetables, which disappear fast.

st.prompt: Astronauts on the space station usually eat tortillas instead of sliced bread. Why?

options.t: Tortillas make far fewer crumbs and stay fresh longer
Bread is too heavy to launch
Bread floats away faster

st.reveal: Crumbs don't fall in space. They drift around and can get into eyes, air filters and equipment. Tortillas barely crumble and keep well for months, so astronauts use them for everything from sandwiches to wraps.

src: NASA, Food in Space.
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, space food collection.

d.try: Hold your nose and eat a small piece of apple, then a small piece of raw potato or pear. Without smell, they can taste surprisingly alike. Astronauts often have stuffy noses in space, which is why many of them start to crave spicy, strong-tasting food.
myth: Astronauts eat crunchy freeze-dried "astronaut ice cream".

The crumbly ice cream sold in science museums may have flown once, on Apollo 7 in 1968, but it has hardly ever been on a space menu. Astronauts on the space station have eaten real ice cream when a cargo ship brought a freezer.

sec.t:
The first space meals were not much fun. In 1962, John Glenn became the first American to eat in [[orbit|orbit]], squeezing applesauce from a tube like toothpaste. Early astronauts also nibbled bite-sized cubes coated in gelatine to stop them crumbling.

In 1965, astronaut John Young secretly took a corned beef [[@food-sandwich-name|sandwich]] on the Gemini 3 mission and offered it to his crewmate. Crumbs began floating around the capsule, and they had to put it away. Back on Earth, Young was told off. Loose crumbs can clog air vents or get into delicate instruments, so space food is still designed to stay in one piece.

In space, the body's fluids drift upwards towards the head instead of being pulled down to the legs. Astronauts get puffy faces and blocked noses, as if they have a mild cold. Since most of what we call flavour actually comes from [[@nose-smell|smell]], food tastes duller.

That is why astronauts often ask for spicy dishes and bring hot sauce. The way your [[@taste-why|tongue and nose work together]] explains a lot about life in orbit.

When Rakesh Sharma flew to a Soviet space station in 1984, he took Indian food with him. The Defence Food Research Laboratory in Mysuru prepared the dishes, so he could share an Indian meal with his crewmates. The same laboratory has developed meals for India's [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] astronauts, Indian dishes packed so they keep for months and can be eaten safely without gravity.

When Shubhanshu Shukla visited the space station in 2025, he took [[@sweets-india|Indian sweets]] and other foods to share with astronauts from other countries. [[@women-in-space|Sunita Williams]], whose father was from Gujarat, has talked about taking samosas into orbit.

Drinks come in sealed pouches with straws that can be clipped shut, because an open cup of water would wobble out as floating blobs. Sticky foods are popular because they stay on the spoon. Astronauts often eat together, strapping food packets to trays with [[@velcro|Velcro]], and the shared meal is one of the best parts of the day.

Water for drinks and rehydrating food is mostly recycled, including water from the air and from urine. After cleaning, it is as clean as good drinking water on Earth, and astronauts joke that yesterday's coffee becomes today's coffee.

text: Chickens come from a wild forest bird called the red junglefowl, which still lives across South and Southeast Asia, from India to Indonesia. About 3,500 years ago, in Southeast Asia, people farming rice and millet began living closely with these birds. Over generations, the birds became tame.

From there, chickens travelled with people: by land along trade routes, by boat across seas, and later on sailing ships to every continent except Antarctica. Today there are more than 20 billion of them, roughly three for every human alive. Hardly any other animal has followed people so far.

st.prompt: Chickens were first tamed from a wild bird. Where did that happen?

options.t: Southeast Asia
Ancient Egypt
South America

st.reveal: The oldest bones known for sure to be from tame chickens come from Ban Non Wat in Thailand, about 3,500 years old. Their wild ancestor, the red junglefowl, lives across South and Southeast Asia, including India's forests.

n.certNote: Most researchers now place the start of chicken domestication in Southeast Asia around 3,500 years ago. Older claims from China and elsewhere have been questioned, and a few details, such as whether chickens reached South America before Europeans, are still argued over.

d.try: Next time eggs are used in your kitchen, rinse an empty shell and look at it under a bright torch in a dark room. You'll see tiny spots where light shines through. These are pores, thousands of them, that let a growing chick breathe through the shell.
myth: Chickens can't fly.
Most chickens can fly short distances, enough to clear a fence or reach a tree branch to roost. Heavy farm breeds fly poorly, but their wild cousins, red junglefowl, fly well.

sec.t:
If you walk through a forest in central or northern India early in the morning, you might hear a familiar crow. That's the red junglefowl. The male looks like a slim, glossy farmyard rooster, with a red comb, golden neck feathers and a long, dark tail.

Scientists who read chicken DNA found that most of it comes from red junglefowl. A little comes from a relative, the grey junglefowl, which lives only in India. The [[gene|gene]] that gives many chickens yellow skin seems to have come from that Indian cousin.

The rooster's famous dawn crow is older than farming too. In 2013, researchers in Japan kept roosters in dim light all day and found they still crowed just before their usual dawn. An internal body clock, not the sunrise, sets them off. In a flock, the top rooster usually crows first and the others wait their turn.

For a long time, people claimed chickens were tamed 8,000 or even 10,000 years ago. In 2022, two big studies checked the bones carefully. Many "early chicken" bones turned out to be younger than thought, or from other birds.

The oldest bones certainly from tame chickens came from Ban Non Wat in north-east Thailand, about 3,500 years old. Researchers think [[@rice|rice]] and millet farming was the key. Grain in the fields drew junglefowl out of the forest and closer to villages, until they got used to people. It's a good example of how [[@farming-began|farming]] changed animals as well as plants.

Chickens travel well. They are small, eat almost anything and lay eggs on board. [[@polynesians|Polynesian]] sailors carried them in canoes across the Pacific, island by island, as far as Hawaii and Easter Island.

Spanish and Portuguese ships brought chickens to the Americas in the 1500s. Some researchers think Polynesians may have reached South America with chickens earlier, but the evidence is still debated.

People have bred hundreds of different kinds. In Madhya Pradesh, the Kadaknath has black feathers, black skin and even dark meat. The Aseel, an Indian breed, is tall, muscular and fierce. Modern meat chickens grow very fast, reaching full size in about six weeks, which raises questions about animal welfare that farmers and scientists still discuss.

India is one of the world's biggest egg producers, and chicken is the most popular meat in the USA. Yet every one of those birds carries the same ancestry, from a backyard hen in Assam to a broiler in Georgia. Each descends from a shy, quick-flying forest bird that farmers let stay a little closer to home, some 3,500 years ago.

text: A dhole is a wild dog of Asia's forests. It has a rusty-red coat, a bushy black-tipped tail and rounded ears. A grown dhole weighs about as much as a medium-sized pet dog, around 12 to 20 kg.

Dholes live and hunt in packs, usually of 5 to 12, chasing deer such as chital and sambar. India has more dholes than any other country. They live in the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], central Indian forests like Tadoba, Pench and Kanha, and parts of the Northeast.
They are [[endangered|endangered]]. The IUCN estimates that fewer than 2,500 adults are left in the wild worldwide, which makes them rarer than tigers.

st.prompt: After a hunt, how does a dhole pack feed pups that are back at the den?

options.t: Adults swallow meat and bring it back up for the pups
They drag the whole carcass back to the den
Pups are left to find their own food

st.reveal: Dholes eat fast at the kill, then trot back and bring up chewed meat for the pups. Every adult in the pack helps, even those that are not the parents. Some also bring food to the adult who stayed behind on guard.

n.certNote: Dholes are hard to count because they roam widely and look alike. The often-quoted figure of fewer than 2,500 adults worldwide is an estimate from the IUCN, and some scientists think the true number may be a little higher.

d.try: Play a whistle-tag game outdoors with an adult watching. One person hides behind a tree or a wall and gives short whistles. The rest must find them only by sound. Try a high whistle and a low one, and notice which is easier to follow.
myth: Dholes are just stray dogs that went wild.
Dholes are a separate wild species with their own genus. They split off from the ancestors of wolves and dogs long ago, and they cannot be tamed like pet dogs.

sec.t:
Dholes are famous for their whistle. In thick forest, where pack members cannot see each other, they whistle to regroup. They also yap, scream, chatter and mew, a much bigger range of calls than wolves.

Unlike many wild dogs, they hunt mostly by day, running prey down over long distances instead of ambushing it. A pack can bring down a sambar weighing more than ten times as much as a single dhole. Working together is everything. Some members chase, while others cut corners to head the prey off, often driving it into water.

Dholes eat fast. A pack can finish a chital in well under an hour. Eating quickly means bigger [[predator|predators]], such as tigers and leopards, have less chance to steal the meal. The relationship works both ways. There are records of dhole packs mobbing a tiger and even driving one away from a kill, though a tiger can easily kill a single dhole.

{{story:jungle-book}}

In a dhole pack, usually only one pair has pups. But the whole pack raises them. Adults bring food back to the den by swallowing meat at the kill and bringing it up again for the pups. The pups also get to eat first at a kill, ahead of the adults.

Dholes do not usually fight over food. [[biologist|Biologists]] have watched them share kills with very little squabbling, which is unusual among predators. A dhole pack also has a strict morning routine. Members greet each other with whines, licks and play, then set off together at dawn. Their teeth are a little different from other dogs' too. They have fewer molars, with sharp shearing edges that help them cut meat quickly.

Rudyard Kipling wrote about dholes in a story called "Red Dog", in [[@jungle-book|The Second Jungle Book]]. In it, a huge pack sweeps through the forest and Mowgli leads the wolves against them. The story made dholes sound like monsters.

For a long time, many people treated them that way. In British India, there were cash rewards for killing dholes, because hunters saw them as rivals for deer. Thousands were shot and poisoned.

Today, dholes face new problems. Forests are being cut into pieces, so packs cannot roam as far as they need to. The [[@deer-india|deer]] they hunt are fewer in many places. Diseases such as rabies and distemper can spread from village dogs and wipe out a whole pack.

Dholes have vanished from roughly three-quarters of their old range, which once stretched from Siberia to Java. India's tiger reserves have helped, because protecting forests for tigers also protects the deer that dholes eat.

They are cousins of the [[@wolves-india|wolves]] that roam India's grasslands, but the two have very different lives. A wolf pack howls across open country. A dhole pack whistles under the trees, and you could walk past one without ever knowing it was there.

text: Most hand sanitisers contain alcohol, usually ethanol or isopropyl alcohol, making up 60 to 95% of the liquid. Alcohol kills germs by breaking open their outer layers and making the [[protein|proteins]] inside them unravel and clump, a bit like an egg white turning solid in a hot pan.

A germ with a ruined coat and scrambled proteins can't survive or multiply. That works against many [[bacteria|bacteria]] and [[virus|viruses]], including those that cause colds and flu. You need enough sanitiser to cover your hands, and you need to rub until it has all dried, which takes about 20 seconds.

st.prompt: Which works better for killing germs, 100% alcohol or a mix of about 70% alcohol and 30% water?

options.t: The 70% mix
100% alcohol
They work exactly the same

st.reveal: Pure alcohol evaporates very fast and can harden a germ's outer layer before it gets inside. With some water mixed in, the alcohol soaks in more slowly and wrecks the germ from the inside.

src: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Hand sanitizer use out and about.

Lab tests on a few germs give that number, but real hands are messier. Sanitiser misses some germs, and does not work well on dirty or greasy hands. Soap and water is better whenever you can get to a sink.

sec.h: What alcohol does to a germ
sec.t:
Many viruses, like the flu virus, are wrapped in a thin, fatty envelope. Alcohol [[dissolve|dissolves]] that envelope the way soap dissolves grease, and the virus falls apart. Bacteria have tougher walls, but alcohol slips through and wrecks the proteins inside.

Strangely, pure alcohol is not the best killer. It evaporates in seconds and can harden a germ's surface into a shell before getting inside. Mixed with some water, the alcohol works more slowly and more thoroughly. That is why many sanitisers contain around 60 to 80% alcohol, not 100%.

Sanitiser feels cold because alcohol evaporates very fast. As it turns from liquid to gas, it takes heat from your skin. This is the same reason [[@evaporation-cooling|sweat cools you down]], only faster.

Alcohol also dries out skin, since it strips away natural oils. So most sanitisers add glycerine or aloe vera to keep hands soft. Gel versions add a thickener, so the liquid does not drip off before you can rub it in.

Using too little is a common mistake. You need enough to wet both hands completely, and you should rub between the fingers, over the backs of the hands and around the thumbs. If your hands are dry in under 10 seconds, you probably did not use enough.

{{story:body-handwashing-history}}

Sanitiser is not magic. It can't get through mud, food or grease, since germs hide underneath where the alcohol does not reach. It also struggles with a few tough germs. Norovirus, which causes nasty stomach bugs, has no fatty envelope to dissolve. Some bacteria make hard-shelled spores that alcohol cannot crack.

Soap works differently. It does not need to kill germs. It loosens them from the skin so running water can wash them away, along with the dirt. That is why doctors say soap and water is best whenever you have a sink. Sanitiser is the backup for buses, school trips and picnics.

Doctors have known for centuries that alcohol fights [[infection|infection]]. In the 1840s, the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed that washing hands with a chlorine solution saved mothers' lives in a Vienna hospital. Many other doctors laughed at him, a sad story told in the history of [[@body-handwashing-history|handwashing]].

Alcohol gels for hospitals became common in the late 1900s. In the 2000s, a team led by Swiss doctor Didier Pittet worked with the World Health Organization to publish a cheap sanitiser recipe that anyone could make, with no patent. Hospitals from India to Africa used it. During the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]] in 2020, sales went up so fast that shops ran out, and even perfume makers and breweries switched to making sanitiser.

Your skin is not supposed to be germ-free, though. Millions of [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]] live on it all the time, and they help keep harmful germs away. And the germs that sanitiser misses are no match for plain [[@soap-germs|soap]], whose clever [[molecule|molecules]] have one end that loves water and another that grabs grease.

sec.t:
[[@art-kathakali-makeup|कथकली का मेकअप]] रंगों के पक्के नियमों पर चलता है। नेक नायकों, राजाओं और देवताओं के चेहरे हरे होते हैं, जिन्हें *पच्चा* कहते हैं। रावण या दुर्योधन जैसे घमंडी, ताकतवर खलनायकों के हरे चेहरों के गालों पर छुरी के आकार के लाल निशान होते हैं, जिन्हें *कत्ती* कहते हैं।

सबसे हिंसक या दुष्ट किरदार लाल दाढ़ी और लाल-काले रंग का भयानक चेहरा लगाते हैं, जिसे *चुवन्ना ताड़ी* कहते हैं। बुद्धिमान वानर देवता हनुमान सफ़ेद दाढ़ी लगाते हैं। स्त्री किरदारों और ऋषियों का चेहरा कोमल, दमकते पीले-नारंगी रंग का होता है, जिसे *मिनुक्कु* कहते हैं।

बहुत-से किरदार *चुट्टी* भी लगाते हैं। यह जबड़े के साथ-साथ लगा एक सफ़ेद घेरा है, जो चेहरे को बड़ा दिखाता है और दीये की रोशनी में उसे उभार देता है। परंपरा से यह चावल के लेप और चूने से बनता था, और आज अक्सर कागज़ की परतें काटकर बनाया जाता है।

{{story:ramayana}}

मुख्य किरदारों के मेकअप में तीन घंटे या उससे भी ज़्यादा लग सकते हैं। कलाकार सीधा लेट जाता है और एक माहिर चित्रकार उसके चेहरे पर रंग भरता है। ये रंग [[mineral|खनिजों]] और पौधों जैसी कुदरती चीज़ों को पीसकर, [[@coconut|नारियल]] के तेल में मिलाकर बनाए जाते हैं।

फिर आती है वेशभूषा: चौड़ा, परतदार घाघरा, गद्देदार जैकेट, भारी गहने और ऊँचा मुकुट। पूरी तरह सजने के बाद कलाकार मुश्किल से बैठ पाता है। कुछ कलाकार चुंडप्पू नाम के एक पौधे का बीज पलकों के नीचे रखते हैं, जिससे आँखों का सफ़ेद हिस्सा लाल हो जाता है और भाव और ज़्यादा असरदार दिखते हैं।

कथकली की तालीम बचपन से शुरू होती है और बहुत कड़ी होने के लिए मशहूर है। छात्र सुबह होने से पहले उठकर कसरत करते हैं और तेल से मालिश करवाते हैं, जिससे उनका शरीर मज़बूत और लचीला बने। वे रोज़ आँखों का अभ्यास करते हैं: पुतलियों को घुमाना, झट से इधर-उधर ले जाना, थरथराना, किसी दीये या उँगली के पीछे-पीछे चलाना।

कलाकार *हस्तलक्षण दीपिका* नाम के एक पुराने ग्रंथ से 24 बुनियादी मुद्राएँ सीखते हैं। इन्हें आपस में जोड़कर वे सैकड़ों शब्द 'बोल' सकते हैं। वे नौ मुख्य [[@emotions|भावों]], यानी *नवरस*, में भी महारत हासिल करते हैं, जैसे प्रेम, साहस, घृणा, डर और अचरज। हर भाव का अपना सटीक चेहरा होता है।

परंपरा से कथकली मंदिरों में और आँगनों में खुले में खेली जाती थी, सूरज ढलने के बाद शुरू होकर भोर तक। अकेली रोशनी मंच के आगे रखे पीतल के एक ऊँचे दीये की होती थी। उसकी टिमटिमाती लौ में रँगे चेहरे दमक उठते थे।

संगीत आता है चेंडा से, जो एक ज़ोरदार बेलनाकार ढोल है, मद्दलम से, जो पीपे के आकार का ढोल है, चेंगिला नाम के घड़ियाल से और छोटी झाँझों से। गायक मणिप्रवालम में बोल गाते हैं, जो [[@malayalam|मलयालम]] और संस्कृत का मेल है।

20वीं सदी की शुरुआत तक कथकली के शाही [[patron|संरक्षक]] छूटते जा रहे थे। 1930 में कवि वल्लतोल नारायण मेनन ने नए कलाकार तैयार करने के लिए केरल कलामंडलम की स्थापना की। यह संस्था जल्दी ही भारतपुझा नदी के किनारे चेरुतुरुती चली गई। आज भी यह भारत के सबसे मशहूर कला विद्यालयों में से एक है। परंपरा से कथकली सिर्फ़ पुरुष करते थे, पर आज महिलाएँ भी इसे सीखती और करती हैं, और [[@kochi|कोच्चि]] में सैलानियों के लिए हर शाम छोटी प्रस्तुतियाँ होती हैं।

text: A government spends money the way a family does, but with far bigger numbers and many more people arguing over it. Each year it writes a budget: a plan of how much it expects to collect, mostly through [[@taxes|taxes]], and how much it will spend, and on what.

In India, the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Parliament]] on 1 February. In the United States, the President proposes a budget, but Congress decides how much each department actually gets. In both countries, elected members must vote before most money can be spent. That rule is old, and it exists so that rulers cannot take and spend people's money just as they please.

st.reveal: Like most large governments, India spends more than it collects, and the difference is called the fiscal deficit. It borrows to fill it, mostly by selling bonds, which are promises to pay the money back later with interest.

myth: A government can never run out of money because it can just print more.

Printing lots of new money usually makes prices rise fast, so each rupee or dollar buys less. Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008 printed money to pay their bills, and prices rose so quickly that savings became almost worthless.

sec.t:
Some spending is fixed before anyone starts arguing. Pensions, salaries and [[@money-interest-loans|interest on old loans]] have to be paid. In India, interest on past borrowing is one of the largest single items. Defence, roads, railways, farm support and help for states come next.

Then there are smaller lines with big effects on children: school lunches through the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal scheme]], [[vaccine|vaccines]], scholarships. The US [[federal|federal]] government spends most on Social Security [[@pensions-old-age|pensions]] and on health programmes for older and poorer people. Much of America's school money comes from states and towns instead. A budget is a list of choices. Every rupee given to a new highway is a rupee not given to a hospital.

Budget day in India comes with traditions. A few days before, officials hold a halwa ceremony, sharing the sweet from a huge pan. After it, staff involved in preparing the documents stay inside the ministry, cut off from phones and visitors, so that no numbers leak early.

For decades, Finance Ministers carried the budget into [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] in a leather briefcase, a habit inherited from Britain. In 2019, Nirmala Sitharaman swapped it for a red cloth folder like a traditional *bahi-khata*, or account book. From 2021 the budget went paperless, read from a tablet.

The very first budget of independent India was presented on 26 November 1947, barely three months after freedom, by R. K. Shanmukham Chetty. The country was still dealing with the upheaval of [[@partition|Partition]], and close to half of the planned spending went on defence.

In America, if Congress and the President cannot agree on funding by the start of the financial year on 1 October, parts of the government shut down. Museums close, some workers are sent home and others work without pay until a deal is reached. One shutdown in late 2025 lasted about six weeks.

India's system works differently, because the government that controls the Lok Sabha nearly always gets its budget passed. The fights happen in speeches and on television, and the lights in government offices stay on.

text: Pocket money is practice. It lets you make small money decisions, and small mistakes, long before the big ones arrive. The basic idea is simple. Before you spend, decide what the money is for.

Many families use three parts: some to spend now, some to save for something bigger, and some to share, such as a gift for a friend or a donation. Keep a note of what comes in and what goes out. Learn the difference between needs and wants. And give yourself time before buying things on impulse. These habits sound boring, but they are the same ones that grown-ups with steady finances use.

st.reveal: Use the rule of 72. Divide 72 by 6 and you get 12. Each year you earn interest on your interest as well as your first ₹1,000, so the money grows faster and faster.

sec.t:
Splitting money as soon as you get it makes decisions easier. If ₹200 arrives and you put ₹100 in Save, ₹60 in Spend and ₹40 in Share, you already know your limit for the week.

The Save jar works best with a goal. "Saving" for nothing in particular is hard to stick to. Saving ₹1,500 for a cricket bat, a book set or a football is much easier, because you can see the finish line. At ₹100 a week, you reach it in 15 weeks. Drawing a chart and colouring it in each week makes it feel real.

sec.h: Needs, wants and the waiting rule
sec.t:
A need is something you really must have, like school shoes that fit. A want is something nice, like a fancier pair with lights in the soles. Wants aren't bad. They just come after needs.

Shops, apps and games are designed to make you want things right now. [[@advertising|Advertising]] uses bright colours, famous faces and "only today" deals to rush you. One defence is a waiting rule: when you want to buy something that isn't a need, wait a day or two. Often the urge fades. If you still want it, you can buy it knowing you really chose it.

More and more payments happen on phones, through [[@upi-payments|UPI]] in India or cards and apps in the USA. That is quick and safe, but it can make spending feel less real. Handing over a ₹500 note feels like losing something. Tapping a phone hardly feels like anything.

If you use digital money, check your balance often. Some families keep part of a child's pocket money in cash, so it's easier to see it shrink. Never share a PIN or one-time password with anyone, even if they say they are from a bank. Real banks never ask.

Money in a piggy bank stays the same. Money in a savings account earns [[interest|interest]], a small payment from the bank for using your money. Interest is shown as a [[@percentages|percentage]] of what you have.

The magic comes when interest earns interest. That is called compound interest. A handy shortcut is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to find roughly how many years it takes to double. At 6%, about 12 years. At 9%, about 8. Starting young gives that snowball more time to roll. In India, children over 10 can open and run a basic savings account in their own name, under Reserve Bank of India rules. Many banks in the USA offer accounts for children that a parent helps manage.

text: A [[tariff|tariff]] is a tax a country charges on goods brought in from other countries. In India, it is called customs duty, and it is collected by [[customs|customs]] officers at ports, airports and border posts. It is paid at the border, by the company that brings the goods in.
Countries use tariffs to protect their own makers, to raise money, and as a bargaining chip in trade talks. But tariffs can also make things dearer for shoppers and hurt exporters in other countries.

quiz.reveal: The importer pays the tariff, so a lower tariff makes Indian shirts cheaper for American shops. That is why India pushes for a "tariff edge" over rivals. A difference of a few percentage points can win or lose big orders, and the jobs that go with them.

news.t: On 13 November 2026, a senior Indian government official, speaking without giving their name, told Business Standard that the United States had assured India its exporters would get better tariff treatment than competing countries. This entry explains what a tariff is and why a few percentage points matter so much.

sec.t:
Most tariffs are a [[percentage|percentage]] of the value of the goods. Here is a simple example:

1. A shop in the USA orders shirts from India worth 1,000 dollars.
2. The USA has a tariff of 10% on these shirts.
3. When the shirts arrive, the American shop pays 100 dollars to the US government.
4. Now the shirts cost the shop 1,100 dollars, so it may raise its prices, buy fewer shirts, or ask the Indian maker for a discount.

If shirts from another country face a 20% tariff, Indian shirts look cheaper, and the shop may buy more from India. That is why countries fight over a few percentage points.

Think of a fair where outside sellers must buy an entry ticket, but local sellers walk in free. The ticket makes it harder for outsiders to compete. If one group of outsiders gets a cheaper ticket than the rest, they have an edge. A tariff works like that ticket, but for goods.

Tariffs do several things at once:

- **Protect** local makers from cheaper foreign goods.
- **Raise money** for the government.
- **Push** other countries in trade talks: "lower your tariffs and we will lower ours."

Some tariffs are a fixed amount instead of a percentage, such as a set charge for every kilogram. Countries also use special extra tariffs, called anti-dumping duties, when they think a foreign company is selling goods below a fair price to knock out local makers. In India, the Finance Minister often changes customs duties in the yearly Budget, which is why the prices of things like phones, gold or toys can move the day after the Budget speech.

Taxes on trade are ancient. Kingdoms charged traders at city gates, river crossings and ports. In India, rulers taxed goods moving along roads and through ports for centuries, and the British charged customs duties too.

In 1930, the USA raised tariffs on thousands of goods with a law called the Smoot-Hawley Act. Other countries hit back with their own tariffs, world trade shrank, and many historians say this made the Great Depression worse.

After the Second World War, countries agreed to cut tariffs step by step. In 1995, the World Trade Organization was set up to keep trade rules fair. Countries also signed [[@free-trade-agreements|free trade agreements]] with each other to lower tariffs even further.

{{story:free-trade-agreements}}

Before 1991, India kept very high tariffs, some above 150%, to protect its young industries. Imported goods, from cameras to chocolates, were rare and costly. After the 1991 reforms, India cut tariffs a lot, and trade grew fast. India still keeps high tariffs on some things, like imported cars and some farm goods, to protect local makers and farmers.

In 2025, the USA put tariffs of up to 50% on many Indian goods, partly over India buying Russian oil. Exporters in places like Tiruppur, famous for knitwear, and Surat, famous for diamonds, worried about losing orders. In February 2026, an interim deal cut the tariff on many Indian goods to 18%, while India kept protecting sensitive farm products like wheat, rice and dairy.

US rules kept changing through 2026, after court cases and new laws. In November 2026, the USA assured India that its exporters would get lower tariffs than rivals such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, once the full deal was signed. [[@usa-economy|The USA]] is India's biggest [[export|export]] market, so these few points matter for lakhs of jobs.

- **Up to 50%**: US tariffs on many Indian goods in 2025.
- **18%**: the tariff on many Indian goods after the interim deal in February 2026.
- **1995**: the year the World Trade Organization began.
- **1930**: the year of the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, a famous warning from history.
- **59.52 billion dollars**: India's exports to the USA between April and October 2026, more than to any other country.

Supporters of tariffs say they protect jobs, help new industries grow and stop other countries from dumping cheap goods. India's leaders have used tariffs to protect farmers and to push "make in India".

Critics say tariffs raise prices for families, make factories pay more for parts, and invite other countries to hit back. They say the best way to create jobs is to make goods better and cheaper, not to block [[import|imports]]. Economists often agree that some protection can help, but too much hurts. People argue about where to draw the line.

**"The exporting country pays the tariff."** The importer pays it at the border.

**"A tariff is the same as GST."** [[@gst|GST]] is a tax on things sold inside India, whether made here or abroad. A tariff is charged only when goods cross the border.

**"Tariffs always save jobs."** They may save jobs in one industry but cost jobs in others that use imported parts or sell abroad.

Tariffs are one of the oldest tools in trade, and they still shape daily life. They change the prices of many things your family buys, from imported phones and toys to gold and edible oil. They also affect jobs, especially in towns that make goods for other countries.

When India gets lower tariffs abroad, its exporters can sell more, which helps factories and farms, and can shrink the [[@trade-deficit|trade deficit]]. Learning [[@trade-world|why countries trade]] and [[@taxes|why people pay taxes]] helps you see why a few percentage points can make front-page news.

text: Latitude and longitude are [[@maps-grids|a grid of imaginary lines]] drawn over the Earth, so that every place can be given an exact address made of two numbers.

**Latitude** tells you how far north or south you are. The [[equator|equator]] is 0 degrees. The North Pole is 90 degrees north and the South Pole 90 degrees south. Lines of latitude run around the Earth in rings, like the hoops on a barrel.

**Longitude** tells you how far east or west you are. Lines of longitude run from pole to pole, like the segments of an orange. The starting line, 0 degrees, runs through Greenwich in [[@london|London]]. Places go up to 180 degrees east or west of it.
[[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], for example, is at about 13 degrees north and 77.6 degrees east. New York is about 40.7 degrees north and 74 degrees west.

st.prompt: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. How many degrees of longitude does it turn in one hour?

15 degrees
24 degrees

st.reveal: 360 divided by 24 is 15. So every 15 degrees of longitude makes one hour of difference in the time of sunrise and noon. India's time line is at 82.5 degrees east, which is 5½ hours ahead of Greenwich.

sec.t:
Latitude was the easy one. In the northern half of the world, the [[@north-star|North Star]] sits almost directly above the North Pole. The higher it appears in your sky, the further north you are. At the equator it sits on the horizon. At the North Pole it is straight overhead.

So sailors could measure the angle of the North Star, or of the Sun at noon, and work out their latitude. Arab, Indian and Chinese navigators in the Indian Ocean used simple instruments to do this hundreds of years ago.

Longitude was much harder. The stars move across the sky as the Earth turns, so there's no fixed star to measure. Without knowing their longitude, ships often had no idea how far east or west they were. Some ran onto rocks.

The answer lay in time. The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. If a sailor knew the exact time at home and compared it with noon where the ship was, the difference told them how far east or west they had gone. But it needed a clock that kept perfect time on a rocking, damp ship.

In 1714, the British government offered a prize of up to £20,000 for a solution. A carpenter and clockmaker named John Harrison spent decades building better and better sea [[@clocks|clocks]]. His fourth, a large pocket-watch called H4, was tested on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761–62 and lost only a few seconds.

{{story:clocks}}

For a long time, different countries used their own starting line for longitude, often through their own capital. In 1884, delegates from 25 countries met in Washington DC and agreed to use the [[meridian|meridian]] through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich. Many of the world's sea charts already used it.

France didn't accept it straight away and kept using Paris on its own maps for several more decades.

[[@time-zones|Time zones]] are based on longitude too. Indian Standard Time is set by the line at 82.5 degrees east, which passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich.

India is wide, though. The Sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh nearly two hours before it rises in Gujarat, yet the whole country uses the same clock time. The United States, which is wider still, uses several time zones.

Today the [[@gps-how|GPS]] in a phone gives your latitude and longitude in an instant, often to within a few metres. Each degree is split into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds, just like time. Ships, planes, delivery apps and rescue teams all use these two numbers to find their way.

text: Sport is full of numbers. Runs, wickets, goals, points, speeds and times are all recorded. Modern teams collect millions more, such as where every ball pitched, how far each player ran and how fast the ball came off the bat.

Teams use these [[statistics|statistics]] to pick players, plan tactics and spot weaknesses in opponents. Broadcasters use them to tell stories. Umpires use them in ball-tracking technology to make decisions. And fans use them to argue about who's the greatest.

st.prompt: A batter scores 80, 0, 0 and 120 in four innings, all out each time. What is their batting average?
st.reveal: Add the runs (200) and divide by the number of times out (4). That's 50. The average hides how up and down the innings were, which is why analysts also look at other numbers, like how often a player scores 30 or more.

sec.t:
In 2002, the Oakland Athletics, a baseball team in California, had much less money than rich teams like the New York Yankees. Their general manager, Billy Beane, couldn't afford star players. So he and his staff looked for numbers that other teams ignored.

They found that a player's ability to get on base, even by walking, mattered more than flashy stats. Such players were cheap. Oakland signed them, won 20 games in a row that season and reached the playoffs. The writer Michael Lewis told the story in the book *Moneyball* (2003), later made into a film. Today almost every major sports team employs data analysts.

When rain shortens a cricket match, how do you set a fair target? In 1997, two English statisticians, Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis, introduced a method using the idea of "resources": overs left and wickets in hand. Later, the Australian Steven Stern updated it, and it became the [[@maths-cricket-dls|DLS method]].

Hawk-Eye, first shown on TV cricket in 2001, uses several cameras to track the ball and predict its path. In the Decision Review System, it helps decide whether a ball would have hit the stumps.

In basketball, statistics changed how the game is played. Analysts worked out that a shot from beyond the three-point line, though harder, is often worth more on average than a medium-range two-pointer. Expected points equal the chance of scoring times the points.

So teams started shooting far more three-pointers. Stephen Curry of the Golden State Warriors made 402 in the 2015–16 season, a record. In football, analysts use "expected goals", or xG, to measure how good a team's chances were, not just how many went in.

Stats can trick you too. A small number of games can make a player look brilliant or terrible by chance. A bowler's average can look great if they only bowl against weak teams. Good analysts always ask: how many games, against whom, and what's missing?

That's the same thinking used in medicine and science, where people learn how [[@statistics-lies|statistics can lie]]. It all rests on [[@probability|probability]], the maths of chance, which says that even a brilliant team will sometimes lose to a weak one.

text: Eid is the name of two main festivals celebrated by Muslims around the world. Eid al-Fitr, the "festival of breaking the fast", comes at the end of Ramadan, a month when adults who are able go without food and drink from dawn until sunset. Eid al-Adha, the "festival of sacrifice", comes about two months later.

On both Eids, families wake early, wash and put on new or best clothes, and go to special morning prayers. Then come visits to relatives, big meals, [[@sweets-world|sweets]] and gifts. In India, many people greet each other with "Eid Mubarak" and a hug, three times.

st.reveal: Twelve months of the Moon add up to about 354 days, around 11 days shorter than a solar year. So Islamic festivals slowly travel backwards through the seasons, coming back to the same time of year after about 33 years.

sec.t:
The Islamic calendar follows the [[@moon-phases|phases of the Moon]]. Each month starts when the thin new crescent is first seen after sunset. Ramadan ends, and Eid al-Fitr begins, when the crescent of the next month, Shawwal, appears.

Because clouds or dust can hide the Moon, people don't always know until the evening before whether Eid is tomorrow. Committees of religious scholars watch and announce it. Some countries now use astronomical calculations. This is why Eid can fall on one day in Saudi Arabia and the next day in India.

Eid al-Adha remembers a story shared by Muslims, Jews and Christians. Muslims believe the prophet Ibrahim, known in the Bible as Abraham, was willing to sacrifice his son because God commanded it. God then provided a ram to sacrifice instead.

On this Eid, families who can afford it sacrifice a goat, sheep or other animal, following rules about how it is done. The meat is usually shared in three parts: for the family, for relatives and friends, and for people in need. It falls during the Hajj, the [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] to Mecca that Muslims aim to make once in their lives if they are able.

Eid prayers are often held in large open grounds or big mosques, because so many people attend at once. At [[@delhi|Delhi]]'s Jama Masjid, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the 1650s, tens of thousands gather in the courtyard and spill into the streets.

In the USA, Eid prayers fill mosques, parks and convention centres. New York City's public schools have closed for both Eids since 2015, so Muslim students do not have to choose between school and the festival.

The Islamic year is about 354 days long, around 11 days shorter than the solar year. So Eid moves earlier on the ordinary [[@calendars|calendar]] every year. Someone who celebrates Eid in summer as a child will celebrate it in winter some years later.

This also changes how hard Ramadan feels. When it falls in summer, the days are long and hot, so fasting lasts longer. In winter, the fasts are shorter. Either way, the first sweet date eaten at sunset, and then the Eid morning that follows the month, are moments many families look forward to all year.

text: Gilli-danda is played with two pieces of wood. The danda is a stick about as long as an arm. The gilli is a short piece, about the length of a hand, sharpened at both ends like a double-pointed pencil.

A player lays the gilli on the ground or across a small dip and taps one end with the danda. It flips up into the air. Then, in a flash, the player swings and whacks it as far as possible. The fielders try to catch it. If they do, the hitter is out. If not, the distance is measured in danda-lengths, and that's the score. It's quick, noisy and needs almost no money.

options.t: Tapping one end makes it spin up like a seesaw, because it's balanced on the ground

The ground pushes it up like a trampoline

st.reveal: The gilli lies on the ground with its pointed ends sticking up a little. A sharp tap on one end makes it flip up, like pushing down one side of a seesaw. Then the player has a split second to swing and whack it as far as possible.

sec.t:
Gilli-danda is played in villages, lanes and open grounds across South Asia, and every language has its own name. In Maharashtra it's viti-dandu. In Karnataka, chinni-dandu. In Tamil Nadu, kitti-pullu. In Bengal, dang-guli. In parts of north India, it's gulli-danda, and in Pakistan and Nepal it's played too.

Rules change from village to village. Some players get three tries to flip and hit the gilli. Some games let a fielder throw the gilli back at the danda laid on the ground to get the hitter out. Children argue about the rules as fiercely as any [[@cricket-history|cricket umpire]].

Similar games have been played around the world. In England, tip-cat was popular for centuries, with a short wooden "cat" hit with a stick. Italy has lippa, the Philippines has syatong, and versions exist in Cambodia and elsewhere.

Some people say gilli-danda may be an ancestor of [[@cricket-history|cricket]], or even of baseball, since all involve hitting an object with a stick and running or measuring. It's an interesting idea, but no written record proves a direct link. Bat-and-ball games probably grew up in many places, the way people everywhere invented tag.

The Hindi writer [[@premchand|Premchand]] wrote a short story called "Gulli-Danda" in the 1920s. In it, the narrator remembers playing with a poor boy named Gaya who was the best player in the village. Years later, the narrator returns as an engineer, an important man, and plays again. Gaya quietly lets him win, and the narrator realises that the friendship of childhood has been changed by the difference in their status.

The story is read in many Indian schools. It shows how a simple game can hold big feelings.

The gilli can fly fast, and a hit can hurt, especially near the eyes. That's why many parents and schools warn children to play in open spaces and keep spectators well back. Some families now use softer gillis.

Still, gilli-danda remains popular. Some states have included it in festivals of traditional sport. And though gilli-danda isn't played professionally, the same basic skill of watching an object and hitting it hard is at the heart of every [[@cricket-bat|cricket bat]] swing.

एक साथ हज़ारों दाने उभर आते हैं। अंग्रेज़ी में इसे "गूज़बम्प्स" कहते हैं, क्योंकि त्वचा पंख नोचे हुए गूज़ (एक तरह का बड़ा हंस) जैसी दिखने लगती है। हम इसे रोंगटे खड़े होना कहते हैं। रोएँदार जानवरों में खड़े बाल गर्म हवा की एक परत को फँसा लेते हैं, जैसे फूली हुई जैकेट। या फिर जानवर दुश्मन को बड़ा दिखने लगता है। हमारे शरीर के बाल इतने पतले हैं कि इनमें से कोई काम ठीक से नहीं कर पाते। इसलिए रोंगटे खड़े होना ज़्यादातर हमारे ज़्यादा बालों वाले [[ancestor|पूर्वजों]] की बची हुई निशानी है।

sec.t:
सर्दियों की ठिठुरती सुबह किसी गौरैया को देखो। वह अपने पंख फुलाकर गोल गेंद बन जाती है, ताकि शरीर के पास हवा फँसी रहे। [[mammal|स्तनधारी]] जानवर अपने रोएँ के साथ यही करते हैं। गर्म, ठहरी हुई हवा कंबल का काम करती है।

हमारे पूर्वजों के पूरे शरीर पर बाल थे, और इस हरकत से उन्हें गर्म रहने में मदद मिलती थी। लाखों सालों में इंसानों के बाल कम होते गए। शायद इसलिए कि गर्म जगहों पर दौड़ते हुए [[@sweat|पसीना]] बहाकर ठंडा होना आसान रहे। पर नन्ही मांसपेशियाँ बनी रहीं। इसलिए जब तुम नहाकर ठंडे कमरे में आते हो, तो शरीर अब भी वह कोट फुलाने की कोशिश करता है जो उसके पास है ही नहीं।

कई लोगों के रोंगटे ऐसी चीज़ों से भी खड़े होते हैं जो न ठंडी हैं, न डरावनी। कोई ऊँचे सुरों वाला गाना, जोश भर देने वाला [[@anthems|राष्ट्रगान]] या फ़िल्म का कोई भावुक दृश्य, किसी से भी ऐसा हो सकता है। वैज्ञानिक इस एहसास को "फ़्रिसों" कहते हैं, जो सिहरन के लिए एक फ़्रांसीसी शब्द है।

दिमाग के स्कैन दिखाते हैं कि जब [[@music-goosebumps|संगीत से सिहरन]] दौड़ती है, तो दिमाग के इनाम वाले हिस्से जगमगा उठते हैं, वही जो स्वादिष्ट खाने पर जगते हैं। खतरे की घंटी भी साथ में क्यों बज उठती है, यह ठीक-ठीक कोई नहीं जानता। एक अनुमान यह है कि संगीत में अचानक आया कोई मोड़, जैसे कोई ऊँचा सुर या नई आवाज़, कुछ पल के लिए वैसी ही प्रतिक्रिया जगा देता है जैसी असल ज़िंदगी में कोई चौंकाने वाली बात। हर किसी को संगीत से सिहरन नहीं होती, और यह बिल्कुल सामान्य है।

लंबे समय तक वैज्ञानिक मानते रहे कि इंसानों में रोंगटे वाली ये मांसपेशियाँ लगभग बेकार हैं। 2020 में हार्वर्ड विश्वविद्यालय की एक टीम को इनका एक छिपा हुआ काम मिला, कम से कम चूहों में। जो [[nerve|नस]] मांसपेशी को सिकोड़ती है, वह उन कोशिकाओं को भी संदेश भेजती है जो नए [[@hair-grow|बाल]] उगाती हैं। लंबे समय तक ठंड में रहने पर चूहों के रोएँ घने हो गए।

यानी ठंड में बाल खड़े करने वाली वही तारें शायद हफ़्तों में एक गर्म कोट उगाने में भी मदद करती हैं। इंसान सर्दियों का कोट तो नहीं उगा सकते, पर हमारे बालों के आसपास की मांसपेशियाँ और नसें शायद अब भी बालों की [[follicle|जड़ों]] को चालू रखने में मदद करती हैं। ठंडी सुबह उभरने वाले ये दाने शायद जितना दिखते हैं, उससे थोड़ा ज़्यादा काम कर रहे हैं।

text: पोलियो एक [[virus|वायरस]] से होने वाली बीमारी है, जो गंदे पानी और हाथों से फैलती है। ज़्यादातर संक्रमित लोग बस थोड़ा बीमार पड़ते हैं या उन्हें कुछ महसूस ही नहीं होता, पर लगभग 200 में से एक मामले में यह [[nerve|नसों]] को नुकसान पहुँचाती है, और इंसान अपनी टाँगें या बाँहें हिला नहीं पाता। इसके ज़्यादातर शिकार पाँच साल से छोटे बच्चे थे।

भारत ने इसे पोलियो के मुँह से दिए जाने वाले [[vaccine|टीके]] से हराया, यानी मुँह में दो बूँदें, जो पाँच साल से छोटे हर बच्चे को बार-बार पिलाई गईं। 1995 से सरकार के पल्स पोलियो अभियान ने टीके वाले दिनों पर लाखों स्वास्थ्यकर्मियों और स्वयंसेवकों को मैदान में उतारा। भारत में जंगली पोलियो का आखिरी मामला जनवरी 2011 में आया।

sec.t:
1950 के दशक में दो अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिकों ने पोलियो के टीके बनाए। जोनास साल्क का टीका इंजेक्शन से दिया जाता था, और 1954 में अमेरिका के दस लाख से ज़्यादा स्कूली बच्चों पर इसे परखा गया। अल्बर्ट सेबिन का टीका मुँह में बूँदों के रूप में लिया जाता था।

भारत ने सेबिन की बूँदें इस्तेमाल कीं। ये सस्ती हैं, इनमें सुई की ज़रूरत नहीं, और थोड़ी-सी ट्रेनिंग के बाद स्वयंसेवक भी इन्हें पिला सकते हैं। इसी से एक ही दिन में बहुत बड़ी गिनती में बच्चों तक पहुँचना मुमकिन हुआ।

पोलियो सबसे लंबे समय तक पश्चिमी उत्तर प्रदेश और बिहार में टिका रहा। बहुत लोग पास-पास रहते थे, [[@water-purify|साफ़ पानी]] कम था, और छोटे बच्चों को बार-बार पेट के [[infection|संक्रमण]] होते थे, जिनसे टीका कम असर करता था। बिहार में कोसी नदी की [[@floods-why|बाढ़]] गाँवों को बाकी दुनिया से काट देती थी।

टीका लगाने वालों ने रास्ते निकाले। वे सफ़र कर रहे बच्चों को बूँदें पिलाने के लिए [[@indian-railways|रेलगाड़ियों]] में चढ़े। वे ईंट-भट्ठों, निर्माण की जगहों, घुमंतू लोगों के डेरों और कुंभ मेले तक गए। वैज्ञानिकों ने बचे हुए किस्म के पोलियो को निशाना बनाने वाले टीके के नए रूप अपनाए। फ़िल्म स्टार अमिताभ बच्चन विज्ञापनों में आए, ताकि चिंतित माता-पिता को मनाया जा सके।

13 जनवरी 2011 को [[@kolkata|कोलकाता]] के पास हावड़ा ज़िले की 18 महीने की बच्ची रुख़सार ख़ातून को पोलियो हो गया। उसकी पोलियो की बूँदें छूट गई थीं। वह बच गई।

उसके बाद भारत ने नज़र रखी और इंतज़ार किया। स्वास्थ्यकर्मी गंदे पानी के नाले की जाँच करते रहे, और हर उस बच्चे को देखते रहे जो अचानक कोई हाथ या पैर नहीं हिला पाता था। जंगली पोलियो का कोई नया मामला नहीं आया। 2014 में भारत और दक्षिण-पूर्व एशिया के उसके पड़ोसी देशों को आधिकारिक तौर पर पोलियो-मुक्त घोषित कर दिया गया।

बहुत-से जानकार कहते थे कि भारत पोलियो से छुटकारा पाने के लिए दुनिया का सबसे मुश्किल देश होगा। उसकी कामयाबी ने दिखाया कि यह कहीं भी किया जा सकता है।

इस अभियान की अगुवाई भारत सरकार ने WHO, यूनिसेफ़, रोटरी इंटरनेशनल और अमेरिका के सेंटर्स फ़ॉर डिज़ीज़ कंट्रोल एंड प्रिवेंशन के साथ मिलकर की। पूरे भारत के रोटरी क्लबों ने पैसा जुटाया और हर टीके वाले दिन स्वयंसेवक भेजे।

अभियान के दौरान तैयार हुए स्वास्थ्यकर्मी बाद में ख़सरे के टीके और दूसरे कार्यक्रमों में भी मददगार बने। लड़ाई अभी पूरी तरह ख़त्म नहीं हुई है। पोलियो अब भी पाकिस्तान और अफ़ग़ानिस्तान में मिलता है, इसलिए भारतीय बच्चों को अब भी बूँदें पिलाई जाती हैं, और उन देशों से आने वाले यात्रियों को पोलियो टीके का सबूत दिखाना पड़ता है।

text: You cannot always tell if something is true just by looking at it. Fake websites can look professional, and [[@deepfakes|edited photos and videos]] can seem real. The best method is to step away from the post and check what other trustworthy sources say.

Ask three questions. Who is behind this? What is the evidence? What do other reliable sources say? Professional fact-checkers do this in seconds by opening new tabs and searching. If no trusted news organisation, scientist or official body backs up a dramatic claim, be very careful before you believe or share it.

st.prompt: Researchers watched expert fact-checkers judge an unfamiliar website. What did the experts do first?

options.t: Opened new tabs to see what other sites said about it
Read its "About us" page carefully
Checked whether the site looked professional

st.reveal: Experts left the page almost at once and searched for what trusted sources said about who runs it. Students and even university professors stayed on the page, read it closely and were often fooled. Researchers call the experts' trick lateral reading.

myth: The 1938 War of the Worlds radio play made millions of Americans panic, believing Martians had landed.

Historians have found that few people were fooled, and there was no nationwide panic. Newspapers exaggerated the story, partly to show that radio, their new rival, could not be trusted. The panic story itself became a famous piece of false news.

sec.t:
In 2018, scientists at MIT in the United States studied about 126,000 stories shared on Twitter over more than ten years. False stories reached more people, and faster, than true ones. Robots and fake accounts played a part, but most of the spreading was done by ordinary people.

The researchers thought false news often felt new and surprising, and stirred strong feelings like shock or disgust. That made people want to pass it on. [[@social-media|Social media]] apps tend to show posts that get lots of reactions, so a shocking lie can travel far before anyone checks it.

A real photo can be used with a false caption. A picture of flooding from years ago, or from another country, may be shared as if it happened yesterday in your city. A reverse image search, where you upload a photo to a search engine, can often show where it first appeared.

New tools can now create fake images, voices and videos, sometimes called deepfakes. Watch for odd details like strange hands, blurry edges or lips that do not quite match the words. Numbers can also mislead, even when they are accurate, if they are chosen carefully. Learn [[@statistics-lies|how statistics can trick you]].

In India, false rumours spread on WhatsApp have sometimes led to real harm. In 2018, WhatsApp limited Indian users to forwarding a message to only five chats at a time, and later marked messages that had been forwarded many times. The Indian government's Press Information Bureau runs a fact-check unit, and several independent fact-checking websites have grown up in both India and the United States.

[[@journalism|Good journalists]] check facts before printing them, a habit going back to the early days of [[@newspapers|newspapers]]. They also correct mistakes in public. A source that admits its errors is usually more trustworthy than one that never does.

Before sharing anything that makes you gasp, pause. Look for the date, the original source and whether a trusted news outlet has reported it. If you are unsure, ask a parent or teacher. Not sharing is always an option, and a surprising number of false stories fade away when nobody passes them on.

text: The Bengal [[famine|famine]] happened in 1943, during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], when Bengal was part of British India. Historians estimate that about 2 to 3 million people died, mostly from hunger and the diseases that spread among weakened people.

There was no single cause. Japan had captured Burma, cutting off rice [[import|imports]]. A [[cyclone|cyclone]] and a crop disease damaged the harvest. War spending pushed prices sky-high. People with money bought and stored rice, while the poorest could not afford it. The colonial government was slow to admit there was a famine and slow to bring in food. Together, these turned a shortage into a disaster.

st.prompt: According to Amartya Sen, what was the main reason so many people could not get food in 1943?

options.t: Prices rose so fast that poor workers could not afford rice
There was no rice left anywhere in Bengal
People refused to eat wheat instead of rice

st.reveal: Sen argued that Bengal still had a fairly large rice harvest. The problem was that wartime prices shot up while the wages of farm workers and fishermen did not. People starved because they could no longer buy food that existed.

n.certNote: Historians agree the famine was caused by a mix of war, a cyclone, crop disease, rising prices and government decisions. They disagree about how much each mattered, and about how much blame falls on the British government in London. Death estimates range from about 2 to 3 million.
