myth: Famines happen only because there is not enough food.

Many famines, including Bengal's in 1943, happen when some people lose the ability to buy or grow food, even while food is still available elsewhere. Prices, jobs and government decisions matter as much as harvests.

sec.t:
In 1942 Japanese forces conquered Burma, now Myanmar, which had sent rice to Bengal. They reached the border of India. Fearing invasion, the British carried out a "denial policy" in coastal Bengal. They removed or destroyed thousands of boats, and moved stocks of rice, so an invading army could not use them.

For fishermen and boatmen, losing their boats meant losing their living. Meanwhile, the government made sure soldiers and war workers in Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], had enough food, which pulled rice away from the countryside.

The economist Amartya Sen studied the famine closely. He grew up in Santiniketan in Bengal and remembered starving people coming to the town when he was nine.

In his 1981 book *Poverty and Famines*, Sen argued that the main problem was not a lack of food. Wartime spending had caused rapid [[@inflation|inflation]]. The price of rice rose to several times its normal level. Landless farm workers, fishermen and craftspeople found that their earnings could no longer buy enough to eat. Traders and some better-off families stored rice, expecting prices to rise further, which made things worse.

Officials in Bengal and in London disagreed about how bad things were. Newspapers were censored in wartime, but in August 1943 the Calcutta newspaper *The Statesman* published photographs that shocked readers in India and Britain.

The British War Cabinet, led by Winston Churchill, turned down or delayed several requests to send more grain, saying ships were needed for the war. How much Churchill personally was to blame is one of the most argued parts of the story. In October 1943, a new Viceroy, Lord Wavell, ordered the army to help move food and run relief camps, and conditions slowly improved.

The famine left deep scars on Bengal. Artists such as Zainul Abedin and Chittaprosad made drawings that recorded the suffering, and writers wrote about it for years.

After independence, India made food security a top priority. The [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] of the 1960s helped the country grow far more grain. Sen later pointed out that no major famine has occurred in a working [[democracy|democracy]] with a free press, because governments that face elections and newspapers cannot easily ignore hunger.

text: The Library of Alexandria in Egypt was the most famous library of the ancient world. It was founded around 300 BCE by the Greek kings who ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great. Its aim was bold: to collect every book in the world.

There was no single moment of destruction. The Library suffered damage in wars, including a fire during Julius Caesar's fighting in the city in 48 BCE. Over the following centuries it lost royal support, scholars left, and its buildings were damaged in more conflicts. By around 400 CE, there was little left. The popular image of one huge blaze is mostly a myth.

st.prompt: Eratosthenes, a chief librarian at Alexandria, worked out the size of Earth around 240 BCE. What did he use?

options.t: Shadows cast by the Sun in two different cities
A very long rope
A map drawn by sailors

st.reveal: At noon on midsummer day the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene, to the south, but cast a small shadow in Alexandria. Using the angle and the distance between the cities, he calculated Earth's circumference. His answer was probably within about a sixth of the true figure, and possibly much closer.

n.certNote: Ancient writers left conflicting accounts, and no building or catalogue of the Library survives. Historians disagree about how many scrolls it held and which events did the most damage.

sec.h: A library for the whole world
sec.t:
Alexandria was a great port city on the Mediterranean. The Ptolemy kings built the Mouseion, a "house of the Muses", where scholars lived, studied and were paid by the king. The Library was part of it.

The kings were hungry for books. Books then were scrolls, long rolls of papyrus, made from a reed that grew along [[@egypt-nile|the Nile]]. Agents bought scrolls across the Greek world. One ancient writer says ships in the harbour were searched, and any books found were copied.

Nobody knows exactly how many scrolls it held. Ancient writers gave numbers from about 40,000 to 4 lakh, and some scrolls held only part of a book.

{{story:paper-invention}}

Scholars at Alexandria edited the poems of Homer and catalogued Greek literature. The mathematician [[@euclid|Euclid]] worked in the city. Eratosthenes, one of the chief librarians, calculated the size of Earth with shadows and [[geometry|geometry]].

The Library helped make Alexandria a centre of learning for hundreds of years.

In 48 BCE, Julius Caesar was trapped in Alexandria during a civil war. He set fire to ships in the harbour, and the fire spread. Some ancient writers say books were burned, possibly in warehouses near the docks. But scholars kept working in Alexandria afterwards.

Over time, the rulers who had funded it lost interest or money. Scholars were driven out during power struggles. Fighting in the 270s CE damaged the palace district. In 391 CE, the Serapeum, a temple that held a smaller "daughter" library, was destroyed.

A later story says an Arab general burned the books in 642 CE. Most historians now think this story was invented centuries later.

India had its own great centre of learning at [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], in Bihar, a [[@hist-first-university|Buddhist university]] that drew students from [[@china-today|China]], Korea and Central Asia. Its library was said to have three large buildings, one of them nine storeys tall.

Nalanda was attacked around the end of the 12th century, and tradition says its library burned for months. Historians debate some details, but the university never recovered. Its ruins are now a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site.

Some [[@libraries|libraries]] have come back from disaster. The Library of Congress in Washington, D.C. was burned by British troops in 1814. Former President Thomas Jefferson sold it his own collection of 6,487 books to start again. Today it is the largest library in the world, with more than 17 crore items.

In 2012, when fighters took over Timbuktu in Mali, librarians secretly carried hundreds of thousands of old [[manuscript|manuscripts]] out of the city in boxes and sacks to keep them safe. In 2002, Egypt opened a new library in Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, with a huge tilted roof shaped like a rising sun.

text: Hyderabad, the capital of Telangana, is famous for many things at once. There are the [[@charminar|Charminar]] and the giant [[@golconda|Golconda Fort]], built by the Qutb Shahi kings. There are [[@pearls|pearls]] and diamonds, the rich food of the Nizams' kitchens, and Hyderabadi [[@biryani|biryani]], slow-cooked rice and meat sealed in a pot.
In the last 30 years it has also become one of India's biggest technology cities, nicknamed Cyberabad. Around 1 crore people live in its wider area.

In tunnels under Golconda Fort
From the bed of Hussain Sagar lake

st.reveal: The diamonds came from gravel beds along the Krishna River, such as the Kollur mine. Golconda was where they were traded, cut and sold, so merchants called them Golconda diamonds.

n.certNote: The Charminar was built in 1591, but historians are not sure why. A popular story says it celebrated the end of a plague; others think it marked the centre of the new city. There is no clear record either way.

The fort had no diamond mines. The stones were found along the Krishna River and brought to Golconda, which was the market where they were cut and sold.

sec.h: A new city and its four towers
sec.t:
By the late 1500s, Golconda was crowded and short of water. In 1591, Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded a new city beside the Musi River. At its centre he built the Charminar, a square building of granite and lime with four tall [[minaret|minarets]]. "Char minar" means "four minarets". Nobody knows for sure why it was built, but it became the city's symbol.

Around it grew the old city's bazaars. Laad Bazaar is known for glittering bangles, and pearl shops line the nearby streets. Hyderabad became a pearl city because its traders bought pearls from the Gulf and from the south, then drilled, sorted and strung them here. During Ramzan, the lanes around the Charminar stay busy late into the night with food stalls selling haleem, a slow-cooked dish of wheat, lentils and meat.

In 1724, a [[@mughals|Mughal]] governor named Asaf Jah declared himself ruler of the Deccan, and his family became known as the Nizams. They ruled Hyderabad State, a kingdom bigger than England, until 1948. The last [[@princely-states|Nizam]], Mir Osman Ali Khan, was once counted among the richest people in the world. He funded Osmania University and hospitals.

At independence in 1947, the Nizam did not want to join India. In September 1948 the Indian Army moved in, and Hyderabad became part of India within days. Later, the state was reorganised along language lines, and in 2014 Telangana was formed with Hyderabad as its capital.

In 1998, the state opened HITEC City, a set of office towers built for software firms. Big international companies followed, along with Indian ones. Western Hyderabad filled with glass buildings, and the city now competes with [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] for technology jobs.

Hyderabad is also a film city. Ramoji Film City, on the city's edge, has been recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest film studio complex in the world. Telugu films made here, such as Baahubali and RRR, became hits far beyond India.

Hussain Sagar, a lake built in the 1560s, separates Hyderabad from its twin city, Secunderabad. In the middle stands a large stone statue of [[@buddha|the Buddha]], about 18 m tall, put up in 1992. In the evening, families stroll along the lakeside road. Hyderabad's food, many languages and mix of Hindu and Muslim traditions are what its people talk about first.

text: Goa feels different because its history is different. While most of India was ruled by the British, Goa was ruled by Portugal, from 1510 until 1961. That is 451 years, longer than almost any other European rule in Asia.

Over those centuries, Portuguese ideas mixed with Konkani, Hindu and Muslim traditions. Whitewashed churches stand near ancient temples, and a local bread called pao is sold from bicycles every morning. The food, music, houses and festivals feel like nowhere else in India.
Goa is India's smallest state, about 3,700 square km. It joined India on 19 December 1961 and became a full state in 1987.

st.prompt: The fiery Goan dish vindaloo gets its name from Portuguese words. What do they mean?

options.t: Wine and garlic
Very hot chilli
Pork and potato

st.reveal: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese dish "carne de vinha d'alhos", meat in wine and garlic. Goan cooks swapped the wine for local vinegar and added plenty of chillies, which the Portuguese had brought from the Americas.

d.try: Make a list of words you use at home or school and guess where they came from. Then check some, such as pav, chabi, almari, balti, tauliya (towel) and girja (church). Many come from Portuguese, and you probably use at least one every day.
myth: Goa became part of India in 1947 along with the rest of the country.
In 1947, Goa was still ruled by Portugal, which refused to leave. Indian troops entered Goa in December 1961, and Portugal's rule ended after 451 years.

sec.t:
Portuguese rule was not gentle for everyone. Many Goans were converted to Christianity, some under pressure. From 1560, the Goa Inquisition, a church court, punished people for following Hindu, Muslim or Jewish practices, and many temples were destroyed. Some Hindu families moved their temples' idols to nearby lands outside Portuguese control.

Today Goa's people are mostly Hindu, with a large Christian minority and a Muslim minority. Festivals of all three are celebrated widely, from Ganesh Chaturthi to Christmas, and Carnival before Lent fills the streets with floats and music.

Portuguese ships carried plants from the Americas, and many reached India through Goa. [[@chillies|Chillies]], potatoes, tomatoes, pineapples, papayas and [[@cashew|cashews]] all came this way. Indian cooking would be hard to recognise without them.

Goan food blends both worlds. Vindaloo comes from a Portuguese meat dish made with wine and garlic, "vinha d'alhos", which Goan cooks changed with vinegar and chillies. Xacuti, sorpotel and bebinca, a layered coconut cake, are Goan favourites. Feni, a strong drink for adults, is made from cashew fruit.

The Portuguese left words behind in Konkani, Marathi and Hindi too. Pav, the soft bread in Mumbai's vada pav, comes from Portuguese "pão". Chabi (key), almari (cupboard), balti (bucket) and girja (church) are others. Many Indians use them every day without knowing.

Goan houses also look different, with tiled roofs, wide verandas, coloured walls and windows once paned with thin oyster shells instead of glass. And Goa follows its own civil code, based on an old Portuguese law, for matters like marriage and property, applying the same rules to people of all religions.

When India became independent in 1947, Portugal refused to leave Goa, saying it was part of Portugal itself. Goan freedom fighters protested for years, and many were jailed. In December 1961, after talks failed, Indian troops entered Goa in an operation called Vijay. Portuguese forces surrendered within about two days.

Goa was a Union Territory until 1987, when it became India's 25th state and Konkani became its official language. Today millions of visitors come for the beaches, but the old churches, spice farms and village feasts tell the deeper story. And across the sea in Mumbai, every vada pav carries a little piece of Portugal, inside a [[@words-borrowed|word that crossed oceans]].

text: Ladakh lies in India's far north, high in the mountains between the Himalayas and the Karakoram. Its main town, Leh, is about 3,500 m above sea level. The air is thin, so visitors are told to rest for a day or two before walking much. The tall Himalayas block [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] clouds, so Ladakh gets very little rain or snow. It is a cold desert of brown and purple mountains, deep blue skies and green fields along the rivers.

Fewer than 3 lakh people live in this huge area. They farm in short summers, herd animals on high pastures and get through long, hard winters. Since 2019, Ladakh has been a union [[territory|territory]], run directly by the central government.

To keep food frozen
As decorations for a winter festival

st.reveal: Streams carry little water in early spring, just when farmers plant. A tall cone of ice has a small surface for its size, so it melts slowly. The engineer Sonam Wangchuk built the first ice stupa in 2013 to release water through the spring.

myth: Deserts are always hot and sandy.
A desert is a place that gets very little rain or snow. Ladakh is a cold desert, with freezing winters and bare rocky mountains. Antarctica is the biggest desert of all.

sec.t:
Almost all water in Ladakh comes from melting snow and [[@glaciers|glaciers]]. Villagers dig channels to lead streams onto their fields, where they grow barley, wheat, peas and vegetables. Apricot trees are everywhere. In summer, apricots are dried on rooftops to eat in winter.

Barley flour, roasted and called tsampa, is a basic food. People drink butter tea, made with salt and butter, which gives energy in the cold. Houses are built of mud bricks with thick walls and flat roofs, where firewood and animal fodder are stored for winter.

Early spring is a hard time. Fields need water for planting, but the streams are still frozen or low. In 2013, the engineer Sonam Wangchuk built a tall cone of ice by spraying stream water into the freezing night air. Because a cone has little surface for its size, it melts slowly through spring, just when farmers need water. He called them ice [[stupa|stupas]], after the shape of Buddhist shrines, and several villages now build them.

Many people in the Leh area are Buddhists. [[monastery|Monasteries]] such as Thiksey and Hemis sit on hilltops, with prayer flags fluttering and monks chanting inside. At festivals, monks dance in [[@art-masks-world|painted masks]]. In the Kargil area, most people are Muslims, and mosques and Buddhist monasteries are both part of Ladakh's landscape.

In winter, temperatures in Leh can drop below −20 °C, and Dras, near Kargil, is one of the [[@weather-records|coldest inhabited places]] in India. Snow closes the mountain passes for months. The [[@india-wonder-chadar-trek|Zanskar River]] freezes so hard that people walk along it, a journey called the Chadar, or "blanket", trek.

Ladakh also has some of the highest roads on Earth. In 2021, a road over Umling La pass, about 5,800 m up, was recognised by [[@world-records|Guinness World Records]] as the highest motorable road in the world. [[@india-wonder-pangong|Pangong Tso]], a long, salty lake about 4,350 m high, changes colour from blue to green as the light shifts. Most of the lake lies across the border in Tibet.

text: A graphic novel is a book-length story told in the form of comics: a series of drawn panels with speech bubbles, captions and pictures working together. Unlike a monthly comic book, which might tell one short episode, a graphic novel usually tells a complete story, or a big part of one, between two covers.

Graphic novels can be about anything. Some are superhero adventures or fantasy. Others are memoirs, history, science or school stories. Some are for young children, and some are written for adults. What they share is the way they tell the story, through pictures and words together, which is the art of [[@comics-art|comics]].

st.reveal: "Graphic" here means drawn or visual, as in "graphic design". A graphic novel can be funny, sad, true or made-up, for children or adults. It just tells its story through pictures as well as words.

sec.t:
A comic page is divided into panels, the boxes that each hold one moment. Between them are gutters, the gaps. In his book *Understanding Comics* (1993), the cartoonist Scott McCloud pointed out that the gutter is where the reader's imagination fills in what happened between two pictures.

If one panel shows a raised bat and the next shows a ball flying over a fence, nobody draws the hit. Your brain supplies it. This is why reading comics is an active skill. A reader has to follow the order of panels, read expressions and body language, and connect words with images, all at once.

Long comic stories existed well before anyone called them graphic novels. Hergé's *Tintin* adventures, first published from 1929, were collected as albums of about 60 pages. In Japan, [[@manga-anime|manga]] stories ran to thousands of pages.

The term "graphic novel" became popular after 1978, when the American cartoonist Will Eisner put it on the cover of *A Contract with God*. The book collected stories about life in a poor New York neighbourhood. He wanted bookshops to treat it as a serious book, not a throwaway comic.

India has a long history of comics, from *[[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]]* to [[@tinkle|Tinkle]]. Graphic novels for older readers grew in the 2000s. Sarnath Banerjee's *Corridor* (2004), set around a second-hand bookshop in Delhi, is often described as one of India's first.

One of the most striking is *Bhimayana* (2011), about the life of [[@ambedkar|B. R. Ambedkar]] and the caste discrimination he faced as a child and adult. It was drawn by Durgabai Vyam and Subhash Vyam in the style of [[@gond-art|Gond art]], from central India. Instead of square panels, the pages flow with patterns, and some speech bubbles take the shape of birds. It showed that a graphic novel can borrow its look from India's own art traditions as well as from Tintin or superheroes.
